nodes.question: What are the overlapping needs in the circumpolar Arctic?
nodes.answer: The overlapping needs in the circumpolar Arctic are for secure and sustainable food and energy.
nodes.paragraph: communications earth & environment Comment A Nature Portfolio journal https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-25-2122-6 Arctic food and energy security at the crossroads Adrian Unc, Majdi R. Abou Najm, Paul Eric Aspholm, Tirupati Bolisetti, Colleen Charles, Ranjan Datta, Trine Eggen, Belinda Flem, Getu Hailu, Eldbj rg So e Heimstad, Margot Hurlbert, Meriam Karlsson, Marius Korsnes, Arthur Nash, David Parsons, Radha Sivarajan Sajeevan, Narasinha Shurpali, Govert Valkenburg, Danielle Wilde, Bing Wu, Sandra F. Yanni & Debasmita Misra Check for updates Arctic food systems blend Traditional Ecological Knowledge with modern, often energy-intensive in uences, triggered by colonization. Food systems future depends on alignment of tradition with innovation, facilitation of resilience and aheritage-driven interaction with the global economy at a pace determined by local communities. The need for secure and sustainable f ood on the one hand, and energy on the other hand, overlap in the circumpolar Arctic, for example in non-traditional land uses, such as modern greenhouse farming. This inter-dependency poses unique challenges, in a region that is a focus point for arange of global changes.

nodes.question: What role does species tolerance play in ecological recovery and degradation?
nodes.answer: Species tolerance to environmental stressors is crucial for both recovery and degradation, as supported by multiple studies.
nodes.paragraph: According to the ARC, different factors dominate at various stages of recovery. Species tolerance to envi - ronmental stressors plays a critical role during degrada - tion phases, while dispersal constraints shape community composition in the early phases of recovery. As ecosys - items mature, biotic interactions, such as competition with established species, become increasingly important. These shifts from abiotic to biotic controls in commu - nity structure and succession have also been observed in empirical studies, such as those examining the relative influence of abiotic and biotic factors on stream mac - roinvertebrate communities (Toskey et al. 2024) and the role of connectivity and seasonality in shaping succession after stream restoration (Westveer et al. 2018). A recent case study by Gillmann et al. (2024a) on a restored catchment supports this perspective, highlight - ing the importance of species dispersal capacity and increasing interspecific competition during recovery, alongside a decrease in species tolerance to organic pol - lution. The strong relevance of species tolerances for both recovery and degradation is well supported by numerous studies (e.g., Chessman 2015; Kefford et al.
